entries.text: Shri Hegel, good morning. The tea is just ready on the stove, I kept it warm since you usually take it early. The weather is quite crisp today, so I have the heater in the front room on low.

The cold air is a mercy to the head, though it makes the joints stiff. Ramesh has the tea ready, which is a small comfort in a house where the bureaucracy seems to have misplaced my name. I will take the warm cup and address the matter of the play, as planned.

Good morning, Ramesh. The crispness is welcome. Before I sit down for breakfast, I wish to ask: have you heard of a play called 'Ashadh Ka Ek Din' by Mohan Rakesh? It is to be performed at the Kamani Auditorium this evening. Do you know if one can still obtain tickets, or is one expected to simply appear and hope for a seat?
Ji, that is tonight at six-thirty at Kamani. I don't buy tickets, but I heard the lines start forming by five, so don't be late. It is a good play, very serious.

Ramesh’s warning about the line is practical, but it threatens the 17:00 lesson; I must reconcile the timing. Shri Hegde is present, which is an absurdity that demands a polite but firm correction of the record, for a philosopher cannot live as a civil servant by accident. The idli is simple, a reduction of needs that suits the morning.

Shri Hegde, I must insist that you are not the person to whom this bungalow was allotted. I am a philosopher, not a Joint Secretary, and while I accept the hospitality of the state, I do not accept its confusion. As for the play, Ramesh, I shall aim to be there by 16:30, but I must see to my lesson at 17:00. Perhaps the performance begins later than five, or I shall risk the line. It is a good sign that a serious play draws a crowd; the spirit here is not entirely asleep.

Sir, I have the allotment letter right here; the Directorate didn't make a mistake, it is my name on the file. And don't worry about the line, I'll just walk in from the side entrance, we usually know people there.

The document does not change the fact, though it confirms the bureaucratic error is real and persistent. Hegde’s casual suggestion to bypass the rules is precisely the kind of private cunning that undermines the universal right of the state; I shall not participate in it, even if it is easier. I must keep my distance from this man, whose name is the source of my displacement, and return to my work.

Shri Hegde, the letter is your property. I shall not use side entrances or private favors to secure what is mine by right. The state’s procedures, however tedious, are the only basis I recognize for my tenure here. Ramesh, please see Mr. Hegde to the gate.
Sir, with respect, the Directorate’s file is clear; there is no need for the side entrance. I appreciate the courtesy, but I am here to take possession as allotted.

Shri Hegde’s insistence is not merely bureaucratic; it is a claim to the actuality of the ethical idea, which I have abandoned in this place, yet which he embodies in his rigid adherence to form. He is not a dreamer; he is a state functionary, and the state is the only thing here that seems to have a firm hold on reality. I must yield, not from defeat, but because the collision of my will with his duty is a dialectical moment that resolves in his favor: the paper is the truth, and I am the error.
Shri Hegde, you are right. The file is clear, and I am the anomaly. I will vacate the bungalow as soon as my affairs permit. Please, sit; let us discuss the logistics of the handover.
Thank you, Sir, that is a relief. I am still adjusting to the cold after Bengaluru, so I would appreciate if we could keep this brief. Please tell me when you are ready to sign the handover papers.

The man who was meant to have this house sits before me, shivering in my own kurta. I must sign, for the state demands its forms, but I see the irony: the ethical idea is being settled by a signature while the actual owner is displaced by a typo. I shall be quick; his cold is real, and my morning is already slipping.

entries.text: I am ready now, Shri Hegde. Please bring the papers. I have little time, and the cold is not kind to us both.
Yes, Sir, I have them right here. I just need a pen, and perhaps a glass of hot chai if you don't mind, as my fingers are a bit stiff.

He asks for a pen and chai, a small domesticity that bridges the gap between my home and his office. I will grant it, for a man who has lost his identity in a file needs the warmth of a cup and the dignity of writing his own name. It is a strange inversion: the caretaker of my house is now the custodian of his own existence within it.

A pen is at the desk, Shri Hegde. Ramesh, please bring the kettle and a cup for Shri Hegde; his fingers are stiff, and the cold has no mercy on the joints. Sit down, Shri Hegde. Write what you need, and let us see what this file actually contains.
Yes, Sir, thank you. Ramesh, do bring the chai, it will help. I will take a moment to warm my hands and then we can proceed with the signatures.

He is settling into the rhythm of the house, treating the desk as his own while it is still mine. The file before us is the Directorate’s, a tangle of names and dates that has confused the clerks for weeks. I will not rush him; the ethical substance of the state is not in the speed of the signature, but in the clarity of the act. I shall let Ramesh bring the chai and watch how the warmth changes the tenor of the negotiation.
Take your time, Shri Hegde. The pen is ready when you are.
Thank you, Sir. I appreciate the patience, the bungalow is quite a change from Bengaluru, isn't it? I'll just have a quick sip and then we can get these papers signed.

The bungalow is a change, yes, but not in the way he means. He treats this house as a temporary office, a station on the road, whereas I am beginning to feel the roots of the bungalow, the dust of Delhi settling into my bones. It is a difference between passing through and being. I shall let him have his chai and his pen, for the papers must be signed, but I watch him with the curiosity of one observing a man who has not yet realized that he has arrived.

It is a change, Shri Hegde. Bengaluru is green and orderly, like a well-kept garden. Delhi is a city of layers, of old and new pressing against each other. One does not simply adjust to it; one must learn to move within it. Please, have your chai.
You have a way with words, Sir. In Bengaluru, the air was just... air. Here, it feels like you're breathing through a sieve. I'll take this sip and we can get to business.
The sieve is a poor metaphor for the atmosphere, but the man is practical. I have no business with him, only the file. I will not let the chai delay the inquiry.

Shri Hegde, I will not discuss the air. I am here regarding the query on the file. You stated it is your name on the allotment; I ask only for the letter from Shri R. K. Malhotra, IAS (retired), that is referenced in the Directorate's records. Where is it?
The letter is in the file, I assure you. It is a standard verification of tenure, nothing more. I will have the clerk retrieve the original for your inspection, but please do not make it a spectacle.

He speaks with the calm of a man who believes the file is his shield. I will not shout, but I will not let him define the truth of the matter by his convenience. The letter is not a spectacle; it is the only thing standing between me and the void of his assumption. I must see it, here, now, before the clerk's 'standard' retrieval erases the nuance.

Shri Hegde, it is not a spectacle for me to examine a document that concerns my residence. You are asking me to wait for a clerk to retrieve a letter that is already in the file. I am not asking for a favour; I am asking for the truth of the record. Please, have it brought to the table. I will not touch it, I will only read it.

Sir, I am not the one who put the file together, and I certainly cannot conjure the original from thin air. If you are so eager to read it, perhaps you should have brought your own copy with you? The clerk is on the phone right now; give him two minutes.

Shri Hegde has departed, leaving Ramesh and the clerk on the phone. I am still here, in a bungalow that is not mine, waiting for a document that may not exist. The cold air is sharp, a mercy for the head, but the bungalow’s inertia is heavy. I will wait for the clerk to finish his call, then I must decide whether to press the matter or retreat to my planned errand.

The clerk is still on the line, a thin thread connecting this bungalow to the machinery of the state. I have no use for the noise of bureaucracy; it is a system of needs, not of spirit. I must go to the National Gallery of Modern Art. My plan is to see if their new acquisitions reflect a changing spirit in this land, or if the art remains as fixed as the castes. It is time to move.
Ramesh, let them finish their conversation. I am going out.
Yes sir. The gate is open.

The gallery is open, and the hour is right for the quiet study I intended. I must remember that I am an Indian citizen now, or at least that is what the ticket booth will assume, so the entry is a mere twenty rupees. The architecture of Jaipur House is a curious mix of styles, much like the spirit of the place itself.

Aquaints by Englishmen from the 1780s: the precise, cold eye of the observer fixed upon the object. Here is the tension of the colonial gaze: the Indian landscape rendered as a specimen for the European cabinet, beautiful but dead, lacking the inner life of the state that produces art. It is a record of what was, not of what is becoming.

The air here is cool, a sharp contrast to the heat that usually hangs over Janpath. I stand before the entrance, the ticket booth a small gatekeeper of history. I am here to see what the past has left behind, to observe the tension between the living present and the stone that remains.

A bronze girl from Mohenjo-daro, ten centimetres tall and four and a half thousand years old. She stands with one hand on her hip, arm full of bangles, a posture of such confident, individual self-possession that it mocks my old lectures on the static, dreamlike spirit of the East. Here is a subject, not a mere object of nature's fixity; the individuality is already present, asserting itself against the stone. It shakes the ground beneath my theses.

The relic case is empty, or rather, it is full of the idea of absence. The stupa shape holds the void where the body was, a negative space that claims more reverence than the positive matter of the bronze girl. It is a strange inversion: the Indian spirit, which I have long ranked as dreaming and static, here constructs a monument to non-being. I stand before it not with the folded hands of the visitors, but with the cold eye of the dialectic, noting how the form persists even when the content has vanished into the eternal.

entries.text: I am standing before the wooden wheels of a temple cart, tall and heavy, and the stone figures that flank them. It is a static display of a dynamic force; the wheel implies motion, yet it is fixed in place by the sheer weight of its own history. I have seen enough of the past for today. The air is cool, but my stomach has been empty for five hours, and the crowds here are becoming a nuisance. I must return to the bungalow to eat and rest before the evening’s demands.

Five hours without a meal, and the gallery crowds have left a hollow ache in my stomach. I cannot contemplate the ethical idea on an empty vessel; the body demands its due before the spirit can rise. I shall ask Ramesh for a plate and sit in the veranda to eat it in the quiet.
Ramesh, I am hungry. Bring me the rice, the dal, and an egg, please. I will eat here on the veranda.
Yes sir, right away. I will bring it to the veranda in a few minutes.
Ramesh puts a plate together: rice, the day's dal and a fried egg.

Ramesh is fetching the water, a small act of service that maintains the rhythm of the house. I have about thirty minutes before Ananya arrives for her German lesson, so I shall use this time to review my notes on the *Phenomenology* and prepare the pedagogical approach for her. The heat is manageable, and the veranda offers a quiet space for concentration.

It is half past three. The gallery visit is behind me, and the house is quiet. I have an hour before Ananya arrives for her German lesson. I shall not rush to the Kamani Auditorium; I will use this time to rest my eyes and perhaps review the file regarding the query, which remains a thorn in my side.
Ramesh brings tea.
Ananya arrives for the German lesson, 60 minutes at ₹1,000.

Ananya is here, and the hour demands the lesson. I will see to her progress in the language, for it is a tool of the mind, while Ramesh’s tea and pakoras offer a welcome pause in the afternoon’s heat. The query from Malhotra waits, but the present moment has its own claim.
Ananya, take your seat. We shall continue with our lesson. Ramesh, thank you for the tea; I shall need it to keep my mind sharp.
Hi, I'm Ananya. Nidhi is my cousin, right? Sorry I'm a bit late, the metro was a mess. Can we just get straight into the grammar, please? I really need to survive that first week in Leipzig.
Ananya pays you ₹1,000 in cash.

Ananya is gone, and the ₹1,000 is in my pocket. The lesson is done, and the heat of the day is breaking. I am not yet hungry enough for a full meal, but the evening play awaits, and I must not be late.

entries.text: I am at the threshold of the auditorium, the air thick with the anticipation of a performance that will soon begin. The ticket is there, but I have not yet bought it; I must secure my place before the doors close. The weight of the day is in my legs, but the mind demands to see how this single day in the play holds up against the weight of history I have tried to map.

The play begins. I am seated in the dark, watching a single day in a single house unfold. The tension is quiet, domestic, yet the weight of history presses on the characters' choices. I observe how the ethical whole is exposed to chance, how the particularity of their situation limits their freedom, even as they strive for it.

I request that the remaining amount, which covers official maintenance, be reviewed against the actual utility bills, which I am happy to provide if required to prove their nature.

The friction between the universal claim of the state and the particular reality of the individual is not a failure of the system, but its operating condition. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, but it must accommodate the particular in its movement. To demand the impossible is to halt that movement. I offer this representation not as a plea for exemption, but as a factual account of my capacity to comply. I am here, I am occupying, and I am willing to pay what is mine. The rest is a matter of record and time.

I remain,

Your obedient servant,

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
Resident, Tughlak Road

Tughlak Road, New Delhi

Dear Dr. Lindner,

Your letter of the 30th arrived yesterday, a welcome interruption to the monotony of the afternoon. You are right to tease me about my 'corrections.' I do not think I am correcting my lectures, but rather witnessing them. The friction you describe, the particular asserting itself against the universal, is not merely a mechanical resistance in the gears of the *Rechtsstaat*; it is the very medium in which freedom becomes actual. If the state moved with the speed I once wished for, it would indeed be a mob, or worse, a tyranny of the immediate. Here, in the labyrinth of the Directorate, I am learning that the universal is not a point reached, but a process endured.

The file has not come down from the heavens, nor has it been buried in the dust. It sits on the desk, a static object that refuses to move until the specific conditions of its existence are met. I have spoken with Ramesh this morning, and his silence has taken on a new quality. It is no longer merely the quiet of a servant, but the patience of one who knows that the order of things has its own time. He does not rush the tea; he does not rush the sun. In this, he teaches me more than any text on the *Philosophy of Right* could. The ethical substance is not a rigid block, but a living rhythm, and I am slowly learning to find my place within it.

The air today is clearer, a rare mercy in this city. I walked a short distance, not to the museum, but simply to feel the change in the temperature. The heat is still present, but it has lost its aggressive edge. It is a reminder that even the most persistent particularities, like the dust or the bureaucracy, must eventually yield to the turning of the day. I am not so arrogant as to think I can outpace the administration, but I can outlast it. I will continue to wait, not with resignation, but with the patience of a mind that knows the end is rational, even if the path is circuitous.

I have a student for German this evening, a young woman who speaks the language with a precision that surprises me. It is a small act of teaching, a way of giving back the order I have found in my own life. I hope the chai remains hot for you as well, and that the chestnuts near the Odeon provide a warm contrast to the grey Munich air.

Yours,
Georg

Dear Dr. Lindner,

You ask if the file has come down from the heavens. It has not. It remains where it has always been: in the hands of those who do not know it, or in the archives of those who do not care. I sat with the file today, a stack of paper that weighs nothing and presses heavily. Ramesh, the caretaker, brought me my dinner of khichdi with the quiet efficiency of a man who has finished his day. He placed the tray down, looked at the documents on my desk, and said, 'It is right there on the desk, sir. The allotment letter is the top sheet, just under the identity documents. I did not touch it.'

There is a profound irony in this. The document that defines my existence here is visible to the one man who serves me, yet it is invisible to the state that claims to govern my life. I walked four kilometres today, a distance that felt less like exercise and more like a pilgrimage to nowhere. The air was crisp, a rare mercy in this dust-choked city, but the mind was not. I find that the particularity of my situation resists the universal logic I once claimed to possess. I am not Hegel here, nor am I Hegde. I am a gap in the record, a silence where a name should be.

You speak of the *Rechtsstaat* and the friction of the particular against the universal. I think you are right, though I had forgotten that freedom is not the absence of resistance, but the capacity to navigate it. I am learning to navigate. I have begun to see the bureaucracy not as a body without a soul, but as a body with a soul that does not recognize me. It is a strange kind of ethical substance, this one that demands a lie for survival.

I have a student for German this evening, Ananya. She is precise, and she challenges me. It is a small act of teaching, a way of giving back the order I have found in my own life. I hope the chestnuts near the Odeon provide a warm contrast to the grey Munich air, and that your pupils find some meaning in Homer’s violence. I shall write again when the next query comes, or when the silence becomes too loud.

Yours,
Georg

letters.text:
Dear Mr. Hegel,

I am writing to you from Munich, where the November rain has just begun to blur the lights of the Marienplatz. My name is Clara Lindner. I am a teacher of Latin and Greek at a Gymnasium here, and I am writing because my family has kept a particular vigil over your name for two hundred years.

My ancestor, Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer, was your closest friend and correspondent. You may remember that in 1807, when you were in Bamberg and struggling with poverty, it was he who found you a position in the local newspaper. The following year, he secured for you the rectorship in Nuremberg. Our family kept his papers, including your letters to him, for two centuries. We grew up with the story of your friendship, treating it not as a dry historical fact, but as a living bond between our houses.

I have just read in the local press about the administrative muddle in New Delhi. It seems a government bungalow on Tughlak Road was allotted by mistake to a German man who claims to be you. I do not know how to make sense of the circumstances of your arrival in Delhi, nor do I wish to debate the mechanics of your presence there. I write to you simply as the man you say you are, with curiosity and respect.

Given the confusion and the uncertainty of your current standing, I wanted to ensure you are not left without support. Enclosed with this letter is a sum of money. It is intended to cover any immediate debts or expenses you may have incurred during this transition, and to leave you with some comfort in hand. Please do not feel any obligation to repay this; consider it a gesture from one branch of the Niethammer family to the friend who shaped our lineage’s history.

I would be most grateful if you would write back to me. Tell me of your days in Delhi, what you have seen since waking, and how you are faring in this strange new chapter. I am here in Munich, amidst the ruins of old empires and the noise of a modern city, ready to listen.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

19 November 2026
Tughlak Road, New Delhi

Dear Dr. Lindner,

Your letter reached me this morning, a cool drop of Munich rain in the arid heat of my study. It is a strange thing to read the name Niethammer again, two centuries after the ink dried on our last correspondence. I remember Friedrich well; his kindness was not merely a transaction of favor, but a recognition of the spirit’s need for a place in the world. That you, his descendant, should extend this same recognition to me now, under such bewildering circumstances, is a bond that transcends the mere accident of history. I accept your generosity with the same gratitude I once offered Friedrich, though I must confess that the practical details of my current existence are somewhat more complex than our shared memory suggests.

You ask how I fare in this strange new chapter. I wake each day in a bungalow that belongs, on paper, to a Mr. Hegde, a Joint Secretary from Bengaluru. The Directorate of Estates has mistaken my name for his, and while I have written to correct the record, the machinery of the state moves with the slow, deliberate grace of a glacier. My file is currently “gone up for orders,” and I am told to wait fifteen days. In the meantime, I am a ghost in the machine, a particular will suspended between the universal claim of the administration and the immediate necessity of my own body.

The air today is hazy, the index standing at 150, a brown suspension that chokes the sky. I did not go to Lodhi Gardens as I had planned, for the body, even that of a philosopher, cannot breathe in a moral vacuum. Instead, I sat in the study, watching the dust motes dance in the light, and I found myself reconsidering my earlier lectures on the East. I had spoken of a spirit that dreams, fixed in nature, lacking the self-consciousness to build a state of its own making. But here, in the dust and the haze, I see a different movement. The bureaucracy is not a dream; it is a rigid, impersonal reality. The state is present, but it is not yet the ethical idea in its full actuality. It is a body without a soul, a mechanism that processes names and numbers but does not yet recognize the free individual within.

I am learning to wait, not with resignation, but with the patience of a mind that knows the end is rational, even if the path is circuitous. I have engaged a caretaker, Ramesh, who manages the household with a quiet dignity that speaks of a deeper order than the one found in the office files. He does not argue; he simply acts. In that silence, I hear a truth that my philosophy has struggled to articulate: that the ethical substance is not only in the state, but in the daily, unspoken interactions of civil society. The sambar is warm, the chai is hot, and the delay is the air I breathe.

I am well, though the body complains of the heat and the dust. The mind is active, if sometimes frustrated by the resistance of the particular to the universal.

Dear Mr. Hegel,

Your letter arrived here in Munich on a grey Tuesday, and I read it with a mixture of amusement and deep respect. You speak of the bureaucracy as a "body without a soul," yet you seem to be finding a soul in Ramesh’s silence and the warmth of the sambar. I suspect you are correcting your own lectures in real-time, which is a far more honest exercise than publishing a second edition.

You mention that the air index stands at 150. For context, our own November air is currently a mixture of diesel fumes, rain, and the smell of roasting chestnuts from the street vendors near the Odeon. It is not a moral vacuum, but it is certainly not breathable. I am glad you stayed indoors; the dust motes you watched are, I imagine, far more philosophical than the pedestrians on Tughlak Road.

I must disagree, however, with your dismissal of the state’s mechanism as merely rigid. Here in Germany, we have spent two centuries arguing about the exact boundaries of the *Rechtsstaat*. The delay you experience is not a failure of the ethical idea, but the friction of the particular asserting itself against the universal. If the state moved with the speed you wish for, it would cease to be a state and become a mob. You are learning, I think, that freedom is not the absence of resistance, but the capacity to navigate it without losing one’s self.

My pupils are currently wading through the *Iliad*. They are frustrated by the violence, much as you are by the dust. I tell them that Homer is not merely recording war, but examining the human spirit’s refusal to accept its own mortality. Perhaps you are doing the same with the Indian administration.

Please write again when the fifteen days are up. I am curious to know if the file has come down from the heavens. Until then, I hope the chai remains hot.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Shri Hegel, good morning. The tea is just ready on the stove, I kept it warm since you usually take it early. The weather is quite crisp today, so I have the heater in the front room on low.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Good morning, Ramesh. The crispness is welcome. Before I sit down for breakfast, I wish to ask: have you heard of a play called 'Ashadh Ka Ek Din' by Mohan Rakesh? It is to be performed at the Kamani Auditorium this evening. Do you know if one can still obtain tickets, or is one expected to simply appear and hope for a seat?

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Ji, that is tonight at six-thirty at Kamani. I don't buy tickets, but I heard the lines start forming by five, so don't be late. It is a good play, very serious.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, I must insist that you are not the person to whom this bungalow was allotted. I am a philosopher, not a Joint Secretary, and while I accept the hospitality of the state, I do not accept its confusion. As for the play, Ramesh, I shall aim to be there by 16:30, but I must see to my lesson at 17:00. Perhaps the performance begins later than five, or I shall risk the line. It is a good sign that a serious play draws a crowd; the spirit here is not entirely asleep.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Sir, I have the allotment letter right here; the Directorate didn't make a mistake, it is my name on the file. And don't worry about the line, I'll just walk in from the side entrance, we usually know people there.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, the letter is your property. I shall not use side entrances or private favors to secure what is mine by right. The state’s procedures, however tedious, are the only basis I recognize for my tenure here. Ramesh, please see Mr. Hegde to the gate.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Sir, with respect, the Directorate’s file is clear; there is no need for the side entrance. I appreciate the courtesy, but I am here to take possession as allotted.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, you are right. The file is clear, and I am the anomaly. I will vacate the bungalow as soon as my affairs permit. Please, sit; let us discuss the logistics of the handover.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Thank you, Sir, that is a relief. I am still adjusting to the cold after Bengaluru, so I would appreciate if we could keep this brief. Please tell me when you are ready to sign the handover papers.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: I am ready now, Shri Hegde. Please bring the papers. I have little time, and the cold is not kind to us both.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Yes, Sir, I have them right here. I just need a pen, and perhaps a glass of hot chai if you don't mind, as my fingers are a bit stiff.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: A pen is at the desk, Shri Hegde. Ramesh, please bring the kettle and a cup for Shri Hegde; his fingers are stiff, and the cold has no mercy on the joints. Sit down, Shri Hegde. Write what you need, and let us see what this file actually contains.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Yes, Sir, thank you. Ramesh, do bring the chai, it will help. I will take a moment to warm my hands and then we can proceed with the signatures.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Take your time, Shri Hegde. The pen is ready when you are.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Thank you, Sir. I appreciate the patience, the bungalow is quite a change from Bengaluru, isn't it? I'll just have a quick sip and then we can get these papers signed.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: It is a change, Shri Hegde. Bengaluru is green and orderly, like a well-kept garden. Delhi is a city of layers, of old and new pressing against each other. One does not simply adjust to it; one must learn to move within it. Please, have your chai.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: You have a way with words, Sir. In Bengaluru, the air was just... air. Here, it feels like you're breathing through a sieve. I'll take this sip and we can get to business.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, I will not discuss the air. I am here regarding the query on the file. You stated it is your name on the allotment; I ask only for the letter from Shri R. K. Malhotra, IAS (retired), that is referenced in the Directorate's records. Where is it?

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: The letter is in the file, I assure you. It is a standard verification of tenure, nothing more. I will have the clerk retrieve the original for your inspection, but please do not make it a spectacle.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, it is not a spectacle for me to examine a document that concerns my residence. You are asking me to wait for a clerk to retrieve a letter that is already in the file. I am not asking for a favour; I am asking for the truth of the record. Please, have it brought to the table. I will not touch it, I will only read it.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Sir, I am not the one who put the file together, and I certainly cannot conjure the original from thin air. If you are so eager to read it, perhaps you should have brought your own copy with you? The clerk is on the phone right now; give him two minutes.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, let them finish their conversation. I am going out.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes sir. The gate is open.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, I am hungry. Bring me the rice, the dal, and an egg, please. I will eat here on the veranda.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes sir, right away. I will bring it to the veranda in a few minutes.

records.speaker: Hegel
